data.title: Word Break
data.summary:
Input: A string s and a list of strings wordDict.
Output: A boolean indicating whether s can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.
Rules: Each dictionary word may be used multiple times in the segmentation.
constraints: s and wordDict[i] consist of only lowercase English letters.
All the strings of wordDict are unique.

data.generator_code:
def generate(rng, n):
    alphabet = ['a', 'b', 'c']
    s_len = max(1, n % 30)
    s = "".join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(s_len))
    dict_size = max(1, n % 20)
    word_dict = list(set("".join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 4))) for _ in range(dict_size)))
    return [s, word_dict]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    s_len = max(1, n % 30)
    s = "a" * s_len
    word_dict = ["a", "aa", "aaa", "aaaa"]
    return [s, word_dict]

data.key_insight: We can determine if a prefix of the string up to index i can be segmented by checking if there is some previous index j such that the prefix up to j can be segmented and the substring from j to i is present in the word dictionary.

steps.title: Convert wordDict to a Set
steps.detail: Store all words in a hash set for O(1) average time complexity lookups.

steps.title: Initialize DP Table
steps.detail: Create a boolean array dp of size n + 1 where n is the length of s, initialized to False, with dp[0] = True representing an empty string.

steps.title: Iterate through String Indices
steps.detail: Loop through each index i from 1 to n to check if s[0:i] can be segmented.

steps.title: Check Subdivisions
steps.detail: For each i, loop through all possible split points j from 0 to i - 1. If dp[j] is True and s[j:i] is in the word set, set dp[i] = True and break early.

steps.title: Return Result
steps.detail: Return dp[n], which indicates whether the entire string s can be segmented.

data.time_complexity: O(n^2 * m) where n is the length of s and m is the maximum length of a word in wordDict (due to substring slicing and hashing).
data.space_complexity: O(n + m_total) where n is the length of s for the dp array and m_total is the total characters in wordDict for the set.

data.generator_code:
import random

def generate(rng, n):
    alphabet = ['a', 'b', 'c']
    word_len = max(1, n // 5)
    words = set()
    for _ in range(min(n, 50)):
        w = ''.join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, min(5, word_len))))
        words.add(w)
    s_len = max(1, n)
    s = ''.join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(s_len))
    return [s, list(words)]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    s = 'a' * n
    words = ['a', 'aa', 'aaa']
    return [s, words]

data.pattern_summary: Dynamic programming breaks a problem down into overlapping subproblems, storing results to avoid solving the same subproblem multiple times.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We build solutions for longer prefixes by using previously computed results for smaller prefixes.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers work best when exploring a sorted array from both ends, not for checking arbitrary string segmentations.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A greedy choice might match a dictionary word early on, but lead to a dead end later without a way to backtrack.

pattern_options.name: Sorting
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. The order of characters in the string is fixed, so sorting the characters or the dictionary will break the problem.

signals.phrase: whether s can be segmented into a space-separated sequence
signals.hint: Implies we are splitting the string at various points to form smaller sub-problems.

signals.phrase: Each dictionary word may be used multiple times
signals.hint: Suggests that the same subproblems will be encountered repeatedly.

data.brute_force_idea: Use recursion to try every possible split point in the string. If a prefix matches a word in the dictionary, recursively check if the remaining suffix can also be segmented.
data.brute_force_why: At each index of the string, the algorithm can potentially branch for every possible end point, leading to an exponential number of recursive calls.
data.bottleneck: The helper function recomputes results for the same starting index multiple times across different recursive branches.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times the helper function is called with the same index value.
Draw out the recursive tree for a string like "aaaa" to see which states repeat.
Think about how you could store the result of helper(idx) the first time you calculate it so you never have to recompute it.

data.overview: The Word Break algorithm uses dynamic programming to determine if a string can be segmented into space-separated dictionary words. It builds up the solution from smaller prefixes, storing whether each prefix is valid in a boolean array.
data.intuition: Think of building a puzzle where each word in the dictionary is a puzzle piece. To see if the full picture can be built up to a certain point, you check if you can reach a valid stopping point right before, and whether the remaining piece matches a valid word.

flow_nodes.label: Loop j from 0 to i-1
flow_nodes.detail: Iterate through potential split points j to test substrings s[j:i].

flow_nodes.label: Valid split found?
flow_nodes.detail: Check if dp[j] is True and the substring s[j:i] exists in word_set.

pitfalls: Forgetting to set dp[0] = True, which prevents the first word from matching.
Confusing the slice indices s[j:i] with standard array indices.
Not converting wordDict to a set, leading to slow O(N) lookups inside the nested loop.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute-force solution recomputes the same start indices multiple times, leading to exponential work. The optimized dynamic programming approach builds the solution from left to right, storing whether each prefix can be segmented in a boolean array. This avoids redundant searches by looking up previously computed results in O(1) time.

derivation.note: Constructs a hash set from the word dictionary once.
Allocates a boolean array of size n + 1.
The outer loop runs n times for each character position in s.
The inner loop runs i times for each step of the outer loop, resulting in roughly n(n+1)/2 total iterations.
Slicing string s takes up to O(m) where m is the max word length, plus set lookup.

data.time_summary: The outer loop runs n times and the inner loop runs up to n times, giving O(n^2) states. Each state performs a substring slice and hash set check proportional to the max word length m, resulting in O(n^2 * m) total time complexity.
data.space_summary: O(n + m_total) extra memory is used, where n stores the dp array and m_total stores the strings in the word set.
data.takeaway: When a problem asks if a sequence can be formed by combining choices and exhibits overlapping subproblems, use a boolean DP array representing prefixes to track reachable states.
mistakes: Forgetting to initialize dp[0] as True, which prevents the first dictionary word from matching at the start of the string.
Using an inner loop that iterates over string lengths instead of split points, which complicates boundary logic.
Failing to convert the list of words to a set, which turns every dictionary lookup from O(1) into O(k) where k is the size of the dictionary.
